The usual background of thousands of brute-force login attempts per day shows up in /var/log/auth.log and normally gets ignored. Today one entry looked odd:

Dec 7 13:43:43 hostname sshd[7412]: Received disconnect from 189.203.240.57: 3: com.jcraft.jsch.JSchException: Auth fail [preauth]

That text looks like a Java exception, which makes no sense on a machine with no Java. Nothing else on the server has changed and no local service is known to use Java libraries. The operator wants to know whether this exception was raised by something on the server itself, which would point to an unexpected component or a compromise, or whether it has some other origin.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The text is not generated locally. On a disconnect, OpenSSH's sshd logs the reason code and the free-form message string that the remote client sends in its SSH_MSG_DISCONNECT packet. The remote attacker's tool is written in Java using the JSch library, and it put its own 'JSchException: Auth fail' text into that message. Fix: No server-side fix is needed. Treat the entry as an ordinary failed brute-force attempt from a Java/JSch-based bot client. Keep key-only authentication, and optionally block or rate-limit the source IP.
solution: (1) sshd's 'Received disconnect from' log line includes the message string sent by the client in SSH2_MSG_DISCONNECT (2) The JSchException text originates from the remote attacker's Java (JSch) SSH client, not the local server (3) No Java component on the server is involved; it is a normal failed preauth login attempt from a bot

grounding.title: auth.log indicates error with JSchException?

question:
We're building a SQL Server failover cluster and needed one more address for a node. The network team allocated 10.40.1.205 and told us it was free. When we entered it in the cluster setup wizard, SQL Server refused it because the address is already in use on the network. To check, I pinged 10.40.1.205 from the SQL server. Replies came back, but they were sourced from 10.40.59.69, not from the address I pinged. The network admin says 10.40.1.205 isn't assigned to anything in his records. Nothing else on the network is reported broken, and we haven't touched any NIC settings on the cluster nodes beyond the initial build. Environment is Windows Server with a standard IPv4 LAN. I need to work out why a supposedly unused address answers pings, why the reply comes from a different IP, and how to find what is actually holding it.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The 'unused' address 10.40.1.205 is still configured on some machine's network card as an additional or alias address, probably left over from an earlier setup the network admin doesn't know about. That host answers for the address and replies from its primary IP, 10.40.59.69. Fix: Run 'arp -a' on the SQL server and note the MAC addresses for 10.40.1.205 and 10.40.59.69. Check with 'ipconfig /all' that the MAC is not one of the SQL server's own NICs. Then have the network admin find the NIC with that MAC and remove the stray address, or allocate a different free IP.
solution: (1) The IP is not actually free; another host has it bound as a secondary or alias address on a NIC. (2) The ping reply coming from 10.40.59.69 points to that same host answering for 10.40.1.205. (3) Use 'arp -a' to get the MAC address(es) behind both IPs and trace the physical NIC. (4) Check 'ipconfig /all' on the SQL server to rule out a misconfiguration on its own NICs.
technology: IPv4 networking / Windows Server (SQL Server failover clustering)

grounding.title: Why was my ping answered by a different IP address than the one pinged?

question:
We run a point-to-point OpenVPN tunnel between two CentOS 6.6 servers in different datacenters. Each has a 100Mbit uplink, and a plain transfer between them outside the tunnel reaches about 88Mbps. Through the tunnel, iperf tops out at roughly 6.2Mbps, consistently.

Server A (10.0.0.1) config: port 1194, proto tcp-server, dev tun0, ifconfig 10.0.0.1 10.0.0.2, secret static.key, comp-lzo, verb 3.
Server B (10.0.0.2) config: the same, but proto tcp-client and remote pointing at Server A.

We suspected a single-threaded CPU bottleneck, since the boxes are Xeon L5520s. top with per-core view during the iperf run shows every core 95-100% idle, with a load average of 0.22.

Idle ping across the tunnel is a steady ~60ms. While iperf is running, ping times become erratic and climb considerably.

Both servers are otherwise idle. Why is the tunnel so slow?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: OpenVPN sets its socket send/receive buffers to a fixed 64KB by default on non-Windows systems. That stops TCP window scaling from growing the window past 64KB, so on a ~60ms RTT link throughput is capped at roughly window/RTT, a few Mbit/s. Fix: Add 'sndbuf 0' and 'rcvbuf 0' to both the server and client configs so OpenVPN uses the OS-managed, autotuned buffers. Additionally removing comp-lzo cut per-core CPU load and raised throughput further, to about 60-80Mbps.
solution: (1) OpenVPN's default sndbuf/rcvbuf is a fixed 64KB (2) A fixed buffer limits the TCP window or scaling, so throughput is bounded by window/RTT on a high-latency link (3) Fix is sndbuf 0 and rcvbuf 0 on both ends (or pushed to the client) (4) Disabling comp-lzo gave additional throughput

grounding.title: Very low TCP OpenVPN throughput (100Mbit port, low CPU utilization)

question:
We're packaging a Symfony app on the php:7-apache base image. The Dockerfile installs some packages and enables mod_rewrite, then copies php.ini and apache2.conf into place. After that it runs `COPY ./ /var/www/html`, followed by three separate RUN instructions:
- `find /var/www/html/ -type d -exec chmod 755 {} \;`
- `find /var/www/html/ -type f -exec chmod 644 {} \;`
- `chmod -R 777 /var/www/html/app/cache /var/www/html/app/logs`

The image builds fine with `docker build -t myname/symfony_apps:latest .` and starts with `docker run -p 8080:80 myname/symfony_apps:latest`.

Once it's running, the Apache log fills up with 'permission denied' errors on the cache and log directories. When I exec into the container, `ls -la` shows the permissions I expect. If I run the same chmod commands by hand from a bash shell inside the container, the errors stop and the app works. We wondered whether we need to add a USER root line somewhere. What is going on?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The files are added in one image layer (COPY), and their permissions are changed in separate later layers (RUN chmod). This combination triggers a bug in Docker's overlay2 storage. The permission changes made in the later layers don't take effect properly at runtime, even though `ls` shows them. Fix: Copy the sources to a temporary directory such as /src. Then, in a single RUN instruction, move them to /var/www/html and apply all the chmod commands. This way the content and its permission changes are created in the same layer.
solution: (1) Content is created in one layer (COPY) and chmod is applied in separate later RUN layers (2) This triggers a Docker/overlay2 bug, so the permission changes don't take effect at runtime despite ls showing them (3) Fix: put the file placement and the chmod in the same layer, e.g. COPY to /src, then one RUN that does mv plus chmod (4) Adding USER root is not the solution

grounding.title: chmod not working correctly in Docker

question:
We are on PostgreSQL 9.3. I set up a read-only login role, XXXX, and it cannot connect. psql returns: psql: FATAL: password authentication failed for user "XXXX". The server log shows:

< 2014-05-20 10:22:24.830 NZST >FATAL: password authentication failed for user "XXXX"
< 2014-05-20 10:22:24.830 NZST >DETAIL: Connection matched pg_hba.conf line 104: "host DATABASENAME XXXX 10.0.0.0/8 md5"

What I have tried:
- Reset the password several times. No change.
- Changed the method from md5 to password. Still fails.
- Changed the method to trust. The login then works.
- Created a brand-new role with an identical pg_hba line. That role connects with its password without trouble.
- Ran GRANT ALL on the database to XXXX. No effect.

Dropping and recreating XXXX also fails: ERROR: role "XXXX" cannot be dropped because some objects depend on it, DETAIL: privileges for database DATABASENAME. \ddp shows default privileges granting XXXX=r/postgres on tables and sequences in the public schema.

How do I find out why this one role can't authenticate?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The role's password validity timestamp (VALID UNTIL / pg_user.valuntil) is set to a date in the past. PostgreSQL therefore rejects password-based authentication for that role even when the password is correct. A known PgAdmin bug could set this value incorrectly when a password was changed. Fix: Check the role's expiry with SELECT usename, valuntil FROM pg_user;. If it is in the past, reset it with ALTER USER XXXX VALID UNTIL 'infinity'; (or a future date).
solution: (1) Correct password plus a failure under md5 or password, while trust works, points to a role-level password validity problem (2) Check pg_user.valuntil (VALID UNTIL) for the role (3) An expired VALID UNTIL produces the same generic 'password authentication failed' error (4) Fix with ALTER USER ... VALID UNTIL 'infinity'

grounding.title: Why can't user login on Postgres

answer: Root cause: nginx resolves the hostname in a static proxy_pass only once, at startup, and caches that IP. AWS ELBs change their IP addresses from time to time, so nginx keeps sending traffic to a stale address until it is restarted. Fix: Add a resolver directive pointing at the VPC DNS server (the .2 address of the VPC CIDR, e.g. `resolver 10.0.0.2 valid=10s;`). Put the upstream URL in a variable (`set $backend "http://...elb.amazonaws.com:3000"; proxy_pass $backend;`) so nginx re-resolves the name at runtime.
solution: (1) nginx resolves the proxy_pass hostname only at startup when it is written as a literal (2) ELB IP addresses change over time, leaving nginx pointing at a stale IP (3) Configure a resolver (the VPC DNS server at the .2 address) with a short valid= TTL (4) Use a variable in proxy_pass to force runtime DNS re-resolution

question:
A CentOS 5.4 OpenVZ/Proxmox container (kernel 2.6.32-4-pve) runs MySQL. It has a primary IP in 208.x.x.x and several IP aliases, some in a different subnet (209.x.x.x). The INPUT policy is DROP. A rule of `iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 3306 -j ACCEPT` lets every client reach MySQL on every server address.

To restrict access, that rule was replaced with three rules: `-p tcp --dport 3306 -m state --state NEW -s <ip> -j ACCEPT` for 208.x.x.184, 208.x.x.196 and 208.x.x.251. The results:
- All three hosts connect fine to the primary IP and to aliases in the same 208 subnet.
- Connecting to aliases in the 209 subnet works from .251, but hangs from .184 and .196. `telnet 209.x.x.22 3306` just sits at 'Trying...'.
- Removing the .251 rule changes nothing for .196, so rule order is not the issue.
- Reverting to the unrestricted rule makes everything work again.

The ruleset also accepts lo, ESTABLISHED,RELATED and the server's own IP, and jumps to a BLOCKED chain before the service rules.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The .184 and .196 client hosts likely also have addresses in the 209 subnet. When they connect to a 209 alias, their routing table's directly connected link route (with its own src address) is chosen. Their connections therefore arrive from a 209 source IP, not the whitelisted 208 address, and the -s rules don't match. Fix: Run `tcpdump -qn port 3306` on the server while connecting, to see the actual source address. Then either whitelist the clients' other-subnet addresses or adjust the clients' routing/source address so they connect from the whitelisted IPs.
solution: (1) The failing clients probably have an additional IP in the server's other subnet (2) Route selection prefers the directly connected link route and its src address over the default gateway (3) Packets arrive with an unexpected source IP, so the -s ACCEPT rules don't match and the default DROP applies (4) tcpdump on port 3306 reveals the real source address

grounding.title: iptables not allowing mysql connections to aliased ips?

question:
After an office remodel done while I was out, I've got a batch of unlabeled Cat5 runs ending in RJ45 keystone jacks at the desks. The far ends all land on patch panels in the server room, and some of those panel ports are patched into the switches. I confirmed which runs are live by plugging a laptop into the wall jacks: DHCP hands out an address and I'm on the network fine.

I then tried to trace the runs with a standard analog tone generator and inductive probe. The runs that are not patched into anything tone out loud and clear, and I traced them without trouble. The runs that are live and connected to the switches give a tone so faint I can't follow it to a panel port. Same toner, same probe, same cable type and building. Is the data traffic on the live lines drowning out the tone, or is something else going on?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The live cables are terminated at switch ports. Modern network devices apply aggressive electrical termination on their ports to cut noise and crosstalk, and that termination absorbs the analog toner signal. Data traffic is not the problem. Fix: Use an advanced toner built for active lines, such as the Fluke IntelliTone. Otherwise, identify the port another way: on a managed switch, look up the laptop's MAC in the MAC forwarding table, or plug the laptop in and out while someone watches the switch link lights. You can also unpatch the run from the switch during downtime and tone it.
solution: (1) Weak tone happens only on cables connected to an active switch port (2) The switch port's termination absorbs or attenuates the analog tone signal (3) Data packets are not what weakens the tone (4) Workarounds: an active-line-capable toner, the MAC table on a managed switch, link-light toggling, or disconnecting from the switch

grounding.title: Tracing a network cable that is already connected to the network

question:
We hardened our Docker host by enabling userns-remap in /etc/docker/daemon.json. Containers now run with a non-root user via `USER containeruser` in the Dockerfile. The image is stock Alpine Linux with no modifications.

From inside one container we tried to ping another container on the same user-defined network and got:

```
$ ping 172.16.0.3
PING 172.16.0.3 (172.16.0.3): 56 data bytes
ping: permission denied (are you root?)
```

We have already tried adjusting AppArmor profiles and granting the container extra capabilities. Neither changed the result. Network connectivity between the containers is expected to work, but ICMP ping from the unprivileged user always fails with the message above. We need to understand why ping is refused and how to make it usable for the container's non-root user.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: On Alpine, /bin/ping is a symlink to the single BusyBox binary, and BusyBox does not carry the setuid bit. When the container runs as a non-root user, ping cannot open the raw socket it needs and fails with "permission denied (are you root?)". Fix: Install the iputils package in the image (e.g. `RUN apk add iputils` in the Dockerfile). This replaces the BusyBox symlink with a standalone ping binary that has the needed permissions for all users. Do not chmod u+s /bin/ping, because that would set setuid on busybox and therefore on every applet.
solution: (1) Alpine's ping is a BusyBox applet (a symlink to /bin/busybox) (2) An unprivileged user needs ping to be setuid (or otherwise privileged), and the BusyBox binary is not (3) Setting setuid on the symlink would apply it to busybox and every applet, which is a security risk (4) Installing iputils provides a separate ping binary that non-root users can run

grounding.title: Can't ping (permission denied)

question:
Fedora 17 host running nginx in front of a uWSGI application, connected over a unix domain socket. If uWSGI is configured to create its socket in an application-owned directory with suitable permissions, everything works. If the socket path is changed to /tmp/MySite.sock, every request fails and the nginx error log shows:

 connect() to unix:/tmp/MySite.sock failed (2: No such file or directory) while connecting to upstream

The operator ran ls -l /tmp/MySite.sock from a shell and the socket file is there. Its permissions give the nginx user read/write access. Both services are running. Switching back to the non-/tmp directory fixes it immediately. Moving it to /tmp breaks it again. nginx says the file does not exist even though it is visible on disk. Why?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: Fedora runs services with namespaced private temporary directories (systemd PrivateTmp). Each service sees its own separate /tmp, so the socket uWSGI creates in its /tmp is not visible in nginx's /tmp. Fix: Don't put IPC sockets in /tmp. Put the uWSGI socket in a shared directory such as /run (formerly /var/run) and point nginx's upstream at that path.
solution: (1) Fedora services get per-service namespaced /tmp (PrivateTmp) (2) nginx and uWSGI see different /tmp contents, so the socket is invisible to nginx despite existing (3) Move the socket to /run (or /var/run) or another non-/tmp directory

grounding.title: nginx unix domain socket error

question:
A Debian server has a public IPv4 address on eth0, and IPv4 works normally. IPv6 does not work at all. Running `ping6 ipv6.google.com` immediately returns `connect: Network is unreachable`.

ifconfig for eth0 shows the IPv4 address with mask 255.255.255.224 and one IPv6 line:
`inet6 addr: fe80::16da:e9ff:feb6:357e/64 Scope:Link`

`route -6` shows:
- fe80::/64 on eth0 and on tap0
- ff00::/8 on eth0 and on tap0
- local /128 entries on lo
- `::/0 :: !n -1 1 5400 lo`, listed twice

Pinging the machine's own IPv6 address only works with `-I eth0`. Without it, ping6 fails.

The operator has read that a router may need to be added to the routing table. They do not know the router's IPv6 address or how to find it. They are not sure why the host cannot reach anything over IPv6.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The interface has only a link-local (fe80::/10) address and no global unicast IPv6 address (2000::/3). There is no usable default route to an IPv6-forwarding router; the only ::/0 entry is an unreachable (!n) route on lo. In practice this means the uplink provides no IPv6 connectivity. Fix: Obtain real IPv6 connectivity. Either have the ISP or hosting provider enable native IPv6, which supplies a global address and a router, or set up an IPv6 tunnel through a tunnel broker. That provides a global address and a default (::/0) route through a forwarding router.
solution: (1) fe80:: Scope:Link is a link-local address only, not routable on the internet (2) A global unicast address (from 2000::/3) is needed to reach the IPv6 internet (3) No valid default route exists (::/0 is unreachable via lo), so there is no router to forward packets (4) Fix is to get native IPv6 from the ISP or use an IPv6 tunnel broker

grounding.title: How to get IPv6 running properly?

question:
We're testing the Postfix instance on a Debian 6 box running ISPConfig 3. Our mail clients (e.g. Mail.app) fail when they use SSL/TLS, so I reproduced the session by hand using openssl s_client against the TLS port. AUTH PLAIN gives '235 2.7.0 Authentication successful' and 'MAIL FROM: lol@lol.com' gives '250 2.1.0 Ok'.

When I type 'RCPT TO: lol@lol.com' there is no SMTP reply. The terminal prints:

RENEGOTIATING
depth=0 /C=AU/ST=NSW/L=Sydney/O=Self-Signed Key! .../emailAddress=postmaster@lol.com
verify error:num=18:self signed certificate
verify return:1

After that, DATA returns '554 5.5.1 Error: no valid recipients'.

Over plain telnet on port 25 the same session works every time: auth, recipients and message delivery all succeed. Only the TLS session seems to lose the recipient. The certificate is self-signed.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: openssl s_client reads a line starting with a capital 'R' as its own command to renegotiate the TLS session. The 'RCPT TO' line is never sent to Postfix, so no recipient is recorded and DATA is rejected. Postfix itself is not at fault. Fix: Type SMTP commands in lowercase in the s_client session (e.g. 'rcpt to:'). Alternatively, test with an SMTP-aware tool such as swaks or smtpc instead of raw s_client.
solution: (1) The 'RENEGOTIATING' output comes from openssl s_client, not from Postfix (2) s_client treats a line beginning with uppercase 'R' as a renegotiate command (3) The RCPT TO command never reaches the server, which is why DATA reports no valid recipients (4) Use lowercase 'rcpt to:' or a dedicated SMTP test tool like swaks

grounding.title: Postfix TLS over SMTP - RCPT TO prompts renegotiation then 554 5.5.1 Error: no valid recipients

question:
Debian 8 (Jessie) host running PostgreSQL 9.5 from the distribution packages. After `service postgresql start`, nothing is listening. Connections over both TCP and the Unix socket fail, and no postgres processes exist. Status output:

```
● postgresql.service - PostgreSQL RDBMS
 Loaded: loaded (/lib/systemd/system/postgresql.service; enabled)
 Active: active (exited) since ...
 Process: 2360 ExecStart=/bin/true (code=exited, status=0/SUCCESS)
 Main PID: 2360 (code=exited, status=0/SUCCESS)
... systemd[1]: Starting PostgreSQL RDBMS...
... systemd[1]: Started PostgreSQL RDBMS.
```

The journal shows no errors. Running the server by hand as the postgres user works fine and the cluster comes up normally:

`sudo -u postgres /usr/lib/postgresql/9.5/bin/postgres -d 3 -D /var/lib/postgresql/9.5/main/ -c config_file=/etc/postgresql/9.5/main/postgresql.conf`

The data directory and config look intact. Why does the service report success but never actually run the database?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: On Debian, postgresql.service is only a placeholder (ExecStart=/bin/true). Actual clusters run as postgresql@9.5-main instances, which a systemd generator adds to postgresql.service's wants directory. The cluster's /etc/postgresql/9.5/main/start.conf is set to 'manual', so the generator skips it and the instance is never started. Fix: Edit /etc/postgresql/9.5/main/start.conf and set it to 'auto', or remove the file, which also defaults to auto. Then run `systemctl daemon-reload` so the generator recreates the wants link, and restart postgresql. You can also start the cluster directly with `systemctl start postgresql@9.5-main`.
solution: (1) postgresql.service on Debian is a dummy umbrella unit running /bin/true; real clusters run as postgresql@<version>-<cluster> instance units (2) A systemd generator populates postgresql.service's wants directory (in /run) with the cluster instances (3) start.conf for the cluster is set to manual, so the generator skips that cluster (4) Set start.conf to auto (or remove it) and run daemon-reload to regenerate the units

grounding.title: PostgreSQL exits after being started

answer: Root cause: The php-fpm unix socket /var/run/php5-fpm.sock is created with an owner, group and mode that the nginx worker user cannot access, so nginx cannot talk to php-fpm. The resulting 5xx error is redirected to a custom error page that does not exist, which is why the client sees 404. Fix: In /etc/php-fpm.d/www.conf set `listen.owner = nginx`, `listen.group = nginx` and `listen.mode = 0750`, then restart php-fpm. The socket should then show as `srwxr-x--- nginx nginx`. Alternatively, run nginx and the socket under the same user (newer Fedora uses `apache` for both).
solution: (1) nginx connects to php-fpm over a unix socket, not a TCP port (2) Socket ownership/mode (listen.owner/listen.group/listen.mode in www.conf) does not allow the nginx user (3) The 404 is masking a backend error, because the configured custom error pages are missing (4) Changing script file permissions does not help; the socket permissions are what matter

grounding.title: Nginx throws 404 only on php scripts using php-fpm

question:
We're testing TLS connectivity to a service on port 9093 (example.xyz) from a Linux box using the OpenSSL CLI:

  openssl s_client -host example.xyz -port 9093

The output contains these errors:

  error:14094412:SSL routines:SSL3_READ_BYTES:sslv3 alert bad certificate:s3_pkt.c:1259:SSL alert number 42
  error:140790E5:SSL routines:SSL23_WRITE:ssl handshake failure:s23_lib.c:184:

The session summary at the end still looks normal: "SSL handshake has read 6648 bytes and written 354 bytes", Protocol TLSv1.2, Cipher AES128-SHA, server public key 2048 bit, secure renegotiation supported, and "Verify return code: 0 (ok)". The server certificate appears to validate. We aren't sure whether the connection actually succeeded or what the alert means, given the verify result is OK. No additional options were passed to s_client.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The server requires client certificate authentication (mutual TLS) and the s_client invocation presented no client certificate, so the server sent alert 42 (bad certificate) and the handshake failed. "Verify return code 0" only refers to the server's certificate checking out, not to the connection succeeding. Fix: Obtain a client certificate issued by a CA in the server's "Acceptable client certificate CA names" list along with its private key in PEM format, and pass them with -cert and -key (adding any needed intermediate chain certs, e.g. via the truststore/CAfile). If the material is in a Java keystore, convert it via keytool to PKCS12 and then openssl pkcs12 to PEM.
solution: (1) The handshake actually failed; no TLS connection was established despite Verify return code 0 (2) Verify return code 0 only means the server's certificate was found OK (3) Alert 42 bad certificate here means the server demanded a client certificate and none was sent (4) Fix is supplying a client cert/key trusted by the server via -cert/-key (check Acceptable client certificate CA names)

grounding.title: Is the alert “SSL3_READ_BYTES:sslv3 alert bad certificate” indicating that the SSL failed

question:
We're building a local Vagrant/VirtualBox box that mirrors production, which runs Amazon Linux 2011.09 64-bit on EC2.

Steps taken so far:
- Launched an instance from the stock AMI.
- Streamed its EBS volume with dd over ssh into a local raw image.
- Loop-mounted that image and created a fresh disk image with a partition offset for a bootloader, formatted ext4.
- Copied the whole root filesystem into the new image.
- Installed grub-legacy (Ubuntu's grub-legacy-ec2 package, not grub2).
- Converted the image to VMDK with qemu-img and attached it to a new VirtualBox VM.

On boot, grub loads and the kernel starts, but early boot dies:

```
dracut Warning: No root device "block:/dev/xvda1" found
dracut Warning: Boot has failed. To debug this issue add "rdshell" to the kernel command line.
dracut Warning: Signal caught!
Kernel panic - not syncing: Attempted to kill init!
Pid: 1, comm: init Not tainted 2.6.35.14-107.1.39.amzn1.x86_64 #1
```

In /boot/grub/menu.lst I've tried pointing root= at the filesystem label and at its UUID instead of /dev/xvda1. The panic is the same every time. What's preventing the root filesystem from being found?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The Amazon Linux kernel (2.6.35.14-107.1.39.amzn1) is built for Amazon's Xen environment, where the root disk is presented as a Xen block device (/dev/xvda1). Under VirtualBox it cannot detect the emulated disk, so dracut never finds a root device, no matter which root= syntax is used. Fix: Replace the Amazon kernel in the image with a generic, non-Xen kernel and boot that from grub. The poster used vmlinuz-2.6.32-38-generic from Ubuntu 10.04 64-bit. Errors from cloud-init trying to reach the EC2 metadata address are expected afterwards and can be ignored or disabled.
solution: (1) The failure is caused by the Amazon/Xen-specific kernel, not by grub or the root= label/UUID setting (2) That kernel expects Xen block devices (xvda) and does not see VirtualBox's emulated disk (3) Fix by swapping in a generic kernel (e.g. Ubuntu 10.04 2.6.32-generic) (4) cloud-init errors about the EC2 metadata endpoint are expected after the swap
technology: Amazon Linux / EC2 AMI migration to VirtualBox/VMware (Xen kernel, dracut, grub)

grounding.title: Converting an EC2 AMI to vmdk image

question:
We're setting up a TLS connection to a registry EPP endpoint (otessl.verisign-grs.com:700) and the handshake keeps failing. To debug it I ran:

openssl s_client -connect otessl.verisign-grs.com:700 -key foo.key -cert foo.crt -CAfile foo-cert-chain.pem -CApath /etc/ssl/certs

Every level of the chain, from depth=3 (VeriSign Class 3 Public Primary CA) down to depth=0 (CN=otessl.verisign-grs.com), prints 'verify return:1'. Immediately after that, the output shows:

error:14094416:SSL routines:SSL3_READ_BYTES:sslv3 alert certificate unknown:s3_pkt.c:1260:SSL alert number 46
error:140790E5:SSL routines:SSL23_WRITE:ssl handshake failure

The output also includes a list of 'Acceptable client certificate CA names'. It reports about 10 KB read and 4 KB written, with TLSv1 and RC4-MD5 negotiated. Since every server certificate verifies, I can't tell what is still failing validation or why the handshake aborts.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The alert is sent by the server, not raised by the local client. It means the server failed to validate or did not accept the client certificate (foo.crt). The client's validation of the server chain succeeded. Fix: Check that the client certificate is issued by one of the server's acceptable client CA names and that it is not revoked. Use tcpdump/Wireshark to confirm the client certificate is actually sent. If needed, check the server-side logs.
solution: (1) Alert 46 'certificate unknown' was received from the server ('sslv3 alert' read via SSL3_READ_BYTES) (2) It concerns server-side validation of the client certificate, not the server's certificate (3) The server certificate chain verified fine on the client side (4) Compare the client cert against the acceptable client CA list, check its revocation status, and confirm it is sent

grounding.title: openssl s_client shows alert certificate unknown but all server certificates appear to be verified

question:
We're trying to connect a Lightsail test instance in us-east-1 to resources in our regular AWS VPCs. In the Lightsail console's account page there is a single checkbox, "Enable VPC Peering", with no options. Every time we click it we get: "Your VPC peering connection failed. You can attempt to enable peering again. If you still can't peer your VPC with Lightsail resources, contact Customer Support." No other diagnostic output is shown. We retried several times over a few hours.

Checks done so far:
- Confirmed that none of our existing VPCs in the region have CIDR blocks overlapping the range the Lightsail instance sits in. The instance is a t2 with a working EC2 metadata endpoint inside a VPC we can't see in the console.
- Tried the operation as the root user instead of an IAM user.
- Tried a second, also long-standing AWS account. Same error.

The region has several VPCs that we built ourselves. There's no obvious way to pick which VPC Lightsail should peer with. Both accounts are fairly old. Why does peering keep failing?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: Lightsail VPC peering only peers with the region's AWS Default VPC, not a user-selected VPC. The older accounts (pre-2013-12-04, EC2-Classic era) have no Default VPC in that region, so peering fails. Fix: Create a Default VPC in the region, or ask AWS Support to enable one for the account. This first requires removing any EC2-Classic and non-VPC ELB, RDS, ElastiCache and Redshift resources in that region. Then retry enabling peering.
solution: (1) Lightsail peers only with the Default VPC in the region; you cannot choose a VPC (2) The affected accounts lack a Default VPC (older accounts supporting EC2-Classic; EC2 Dashboard shows Supported Platforms EC2 and VPC with no Default VPC) (3) Remedy is to create a Default VPC or have AWS Support enable one, which requires no EC2-Classic resources in that region

grounding.title: Can't establish VPC peering connection from Amazon Lightsail

question:
New Ubuntu 12.04 web server running Apache 2.2.22 with mod_ssl. About a dozen virtual hosts were set up, each in its own file under sites-available, and all were enabled in one pass with `a2ensite *`. The config reload failed. After a full restart, error.log showed:

Oops, no RSA or DSA server certificate found for 'server.host.name:0'?!

The vhost named in the message looks correct. Its SSLCertificateFile and SSLCertificateKeyFile directives point to files that exist. Searching for the error mostly turns up old reports and an Apache bugzilla entry (bug 31709) that has since been fixed, and none of those suggestions helped. Apache will not start while all of the sites are enabled.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: Two of the newly enabled virtual host config files declared the same ServerName value. The duplicate made Apache/mod_ssl fail with the misleading certificate error, which names a host in a different file from the one actually at fault. Fix: Find the conflicting configuration by disabling all sites and re-enabling them a few at a time until the error comes back. Then correct the duplicated ServerName in the offending file and restart Apache.
solution: (1) The cause is duplicate ServerName values in two vhost config files. (2) The hostname in the error message is misleading; the faulty file is a different one. (3) Bisect by disabling all sites and re-enabling them a few at a time to isolate the conflict. (4) Making the ServerName values unique lets Apache start.

grounding.title: Oops, no RSA or DSA server certificate found for 'server.host.name:0'?

question:
Local dev cluster running on minikube (VirtualBox driver). When I tail pod logs with `kubectl logs -f <pod>`, the stream intermittently dies. It happens unpredictably, both on pods in our own namespace and on kube-system pods such as the nginx ingress controller. Output looks normal right up to the end, then the command stops with:

failed to watch file "/var/log/pods/kube-system_nginx-ingress-controller-586cdc477c-95pgh_4b8310a4-5f9b-11e9-9666-0800270e7244/nginx-ingress-controller/1.log": no space left on device

The pods themselves look healthy: no restarts and no errors in their output. Some log tails work fine and others fail with this message. It is not consistent per pod. Re-running the command sometimes succeeds. What is actually causing this, and how do I make it stop?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The minikube node has run out of inotify watches. The fs.inotify.max_user_watches sysctl is set too low, often autotuned to something small like 8192 on a low-memory VM. When the watch limit is exhausted, the follow-mode log watch fails with ENOSPC ('no space left on device') even though disk space is fine. Fix: Use `minikube ssh` to get onto the node and check `sysctl fs.inotify.max_user_watches`. Raise the value, for example by doubling it repeatedly, until the errors stop.
solution: (1) The 'no space left on device' message refers to inotify watch exhaustion, not disk space. (2) The limit is controlled by the fs.inotify.max_user_watches sysctl on the node. (3) The default is autotuned by memory, so it can be very low (e.g. 8192) on a small minikube VM. (4) Fix: run minikube ssh and increase max_user_watches, e.g. by doubling it.

grounding.title: minikube/k8s/kubectl "failed to watch file [ ... ]: no space left on device"

question:
We have an Addonics NAS Adapter (hardware NAS running Samba; no access to its logs) serving a share at \\192.168.0.20\Smd. From existing Windows XP and Windows Vista machines, `net use l: \\192.168.0.20\Smd` prompts for username/password and maps fine. A newly purchased Windows 7 PC running the identical `net use` command with the exact same credentials fails with "The specified network password is not correct." Mapping through Explorer's Map Network Drive gives the same error. We synchronized the clock on the Windows 7 box with the other machines and retried; no change. Credentials have been double-checked and work everywhere else. Need to find out why only the Windows 7 client is rejected and how to get it to connect.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: Windows 7 (like Vista/2008 R2) defaults to sending only NTLMv2 authentication responses, and the older Samba implementation on the NAS does not support NTLMv2, so it rejects the login as a bad password. Fix: On the Windows 7 client, open secpol.msc > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' and change it from 'Send NTLMv2 response only' to 'Send LM & NTLM - use NTLMv2 session security if negotiated' (or set HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\LmCompatibilityLevel from 3 to 1), then reboot if needed.
solution: (1) Windows 7 defaults to NTLMv2-only authentication (2) The NAS's old Samba version does not support NTLMv2 and returns a password failure (3) Lower the LAN Manager authentication level / LmCompatibilityLevel to allow LM & NTLM (v1) (4) Change via secpol.msc or registry Lsa\LmCompatibilityLevel=1
technology: Windows 7 SMB client / Samba NAS authentication

grounding.title: Windows7 - “The specified network password is not correct.” when the password is in fact correct

question:
We upgraded our AKS cluster from Kubernetes 1.23.8 to 1.24.3, and ingress traffic from outside the cluster stopped working. ingress-nginx is deployed through a Helm release, chart version 4.2.5.

No errors appear in cluster events, and the ingress-nginx controller pod logs show nothing unusual. Inside the cluster everything behaves normally: curling the web apps from other pods works, and the controller routes requests fine. From the internet, every port on the ingress public IP looks closed.

To rule out our own configuration, we built fresh, plain AKS clusters and ran a stock `helm install quickstart ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx` on each. On 1.23.8 external access works. On 1.24.0 and 1.24.3 it does not. The controller Service of type LoadBalancer still gets its public IP on every version. We suspect some ingress or controller setting needs to change for 1.24, but we have not identified which.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: Starting with AKS/Kubernetes 1.24, the Azure load balancer health probes for the ingress-nginx LoadBalancer service use HTTP/HTTPS instead of TCP, probing a path the controller does not answer successfully. The probes fail, so Azure marks the backends unhealthy and drops all external traffic. Fix: Add the annotation service.beta.kubernetes.io/azure-load-balancer-health-probe-request-path: /healthz to the ingress-nginx controller service via Helm values (controller.service.annotations). Alternatively, switch the LB health probes to TCP.
solution: (1) Azure Load Balancer health probes changed from TCP to HTTP/HTTPS for AKS 1.24+ (2) The probes fail against ingress-nginx, so the LB considers backends unhealthy and blocks external traffic (3) Fix: set the azure-load-balancer-health-probe-request-path annotation to /healthz on the controller service (or use TCP probes)

grounding.title: Kubernetes v1.24.3 upgrade broke ingress-nginx

answer: Root cause: The root directive is defined only inside location /, so it does not apply to the location ~ \.php$ block. The included fastcgi_params most likely sets SCRIPT_FILENAME to $document_root$fastcgi_script_name, and because it is included after the custom line it overrides it. With no proper document root, PHP-FPM receives the wrong script path and returns a tiny error response, which Chrome replaces with its own error page. Fix: Move the root /var/www/website directive up to the server level so every location, including the PHP one, inherits it. Use fastcgi_param SCRIPT_FILENAME $document_root$fastcgi_script_name with include fastcgi_params.
solution: (1) root is set only in location / and is not inherited by the separate PHP location (2) SCRIPT_FILENAME, likely from fastcgi_params via $document_root, resolves to a wrong path, so FPM cannot find the script (3) Moving root to the server context fixes it (4) Chrome's 'link appears to be broken' page hides the small (<512 byte) error response, which is why permission changes didn't help

grounding.title: NGINX not executing PHP files

question:
CentOS 6.5 host running nginx 1.4.4. Running `sudo service nginx stop` just prints `Stopping nginx: [FAILED]`. nginx.conf contains `pid /var/run/nginx.pid;`, but no such file exists in /var/run. An older locate database listed both /var/run/nginx.pid and /var/run/nginx.pid.oldbin; after running updatedb, neither shows up.

`ps -ef | grep nginx` shows:
```
root     19506     1  0  2013 ?  00:00:00 nginx: master process /usr/sbin/nginx -c /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
ironsand 19507 19506  0  2013 ?  00:00:25 nginx: worker process
```

`sudo service nginx restart` produces:
```
Stopping nginx: [FAILED]
Starting nginx: nginx: [emerg] bind() to 0.0.0.0:80 failed (98: Address already in use)
... (repeated)
nginx: [emerg] still could not bind()
 [FAILED]
```
The same bind errors also appear in /var/log/nginx/error.log. We need to get nginx stopped and restarted cleanly.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: An nginx master process (PID 19506) was left running from an improper shutdown, and its PID file /var/run/nginx.pid no longer exists. The init script relies on that file, so it can't find or stop the process. The orphaned master still holds port 80, which makes every new start fail with 'Address already in use'. Fix: Find the nginx master PID with `ps -ef | grep nginx` and kill it manually (e.g. `kill -9 19506`). Then confirm with `ps` and `netstat -tulpn | grep 80` that nothing is left on port 80, and that /var is readable and writable. Finally run `service nginx start`.
solution: (1) An old nginx master process is still running even though the service reports stop failure (2) The PID file referenced in nginx.conf is missing, so the init script cannot stop the process (3) The leftover process holds port 80, causing the bind() 'Address already in use' errors on start (4) Kill the master process manually, verify port 80 is free, then start nginx via the service

grounding.title: Nginx fails to stop and nginx.pid is missing

question:
We're moving app-to-database traffic onto TLS. The web tier is a CentOS 5 host and the database is MySQL on FreeBSD, using DigiCert intermediate-issued certificates. The [mysqld] section of my.cnf sets port 3306, plus ssl, ssl-capath=/opt/mysql/pki/CA, ssl-cert=/opt/mysql/pki/server-cert.pem and ssl-key=/opt/mysql/pki/server-key.pem. mysqld starts cleanly with nothing in the error log.

From the web host, `mysql -h mysql.example.org -u user -p` returns `ERROR 2026 (HY000): SSL connection error`. To look at the handshake directly, I ran `openssl s_client -connect mysql.example.org:3306 </dev/null`. It prints CONNECTED(00000003) and then `error:140770FC:SSL routines:SSL23_GET_SERVER_HELLO:unknown protocol:s23_clnt.c:588`. That looks like the server isn't speaking TLS on that port at all.

The same s_client command against our LDAPS server on 636 and our HTTPS server on 443 works fine and prints the full certificate chains. I need to know whether the openssl probe result means the MySQL server isn't doing TLS, or whether the test itself is flawed.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: MySQL doesn't start TLS when the TCP connection opens. The server first sends a plaintext MySQL protocol greeting and upgrades to TLS inside the MySQL protocol, STARTTLS-style. A plain `openssl s_client -connect host:3306` therefore receives non-TLS bytes and reports 'unknown protocol'. That result doesn't show that the server's SSL setup is broken. Fix: Use an OpenSSL build that understands MySQL's in-protocol TLS upgrade (OpenSSL 1.1.1 or later). Run `openssl s_client -starttls mysql -connect mysql.example.org:3306 -CAfile <ca.pem>`, which completes the MySQL negotiation before the TLS handshake and shows the certificate chain and verify result.
solution: (1) MySQL negotiates TLS within its own protocol (STARTTLS-like), not as raw TLS on connect (2) A plain s_client probe to 3306 gets the plaintext MySQL greeting and reports SSL23_GET_SERVER_HELLO unknown protocol (3) LDAPS on 636 and HTTPS on 443 speak TLS immediately, which is why the same probe works there (4) Use `openssl s_client -starttls mysql`, available in OpenSSL 1.1.1+

grounding.title: Can OpenSSL be used to debug an SSL connection to a MySQL server?

question:
On an Ubuntu EC2 instance on AWS running Apache, I need HTTPS working, so I tried to add SSL support to Apache. Coming from a RHEL/CentOS background, I ran `apt-get install mod_ssl`. Apt read the package lists, built the dependency tree and read state information, then failed with:

```
E: Unable to locate package mod_ssl
```

Running `apt-get update` did not change anything. Apache itself is installed and serving HTTP fine. I can't find any repository that provides this package and don't know how to get SSL support into Apache on this box. How do I get the SSL module installed?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: On Ubuntu/Debian there is no separate mod_ssl package. mod_ssl.so is already bundled in the Apache common package (e.g. apache2.2-common), so apt cannot find a package by that name. Fix: Confirm the module is present with `dpkg -S mod_ssl.so`, which shows it under /usr/lib/apache2/modules/ from the apache common package. Then enable it with `a2enmod ssl` and restart Apache.
solution: (1) mod_ssl is not a separate package on Ubuntu/Debian (2) the module ships with the Apache common package (apache2.2-common), verifiable with dpkg -S mod_ssl.so (3) enable it with a2enmod ssl instead of installing it
technology: Apache HTTP Server on Ubuntu (AWS EC2)

grounding.title: AWS installing mod_ssl on apache

question:
We run a small Redis 3.2.5 cluster. 192.168.0.14:6379 is a master that owns all slots (0-16383). 192.168.0.15:6379 is its replica. 192.168.0.16:6379 is a second master with no slots assigned. Our understanding was that any cluster node can take a query and route it to the right place.

When we connect to 192.168.0.16 with redis-cli and run commands, nothing gets stored or read:
```
192.168.0.16:6379> set myKey myValue
(error) MOVED 16281 192.168.0.14:6379
192.168.0.16:6379> get myKey
(error) MOVED 16281 192.168.0.14:6379
```
We then connected to 192.168.0.14 and ran `get myKey`, which returned `(nil)`. So the write never landed anywhere. The cluster otherwise looks healthy. What is going wrong with these requests?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The MOVED error is the redirect itself. Redis Cluster nodes do not proxy or forward commands; they tell the client which node owns the slot. The client is responsible for reconnecting there and retrying. redis-cli was started without cluster mode, so it did not follow the redirect and the SET never ran. Fix: Use a cluster-aware client that follows MOVED/ASK redirects. With redis-cli, start it with the -c option (e.g. `redis-cli -c -h 192.168.0.16 -p 6379`) so it automatically follows the redirect to 192.168.0.14.
solution: (1) MOVED is a redirect response telling the client which node owns the slot (2) Redis Cluster servers do not forward or proxy requests to the owning node (3) The client must reconnect to the indicated node and retry (4) redis-cli requires the -c flag to follow cluster redirects

grounding.title: Redis Cluster: (error) MOVED

question:
We're consolidating several web apps behind Apache 2.2 on one host, and every app has to be served over HTTPS. The first app is a Tomcat instance that already serves HTTPS directly on port 8443, and that works fine. I created this vhost to front it on port 443:

<VirtualHost 1.2.3.4:443>
 ServerName host.example.org
 <Proxy *> Order deny,allow / Allow from all </Proxy>
 SSLProxyEngine On
 ProxyRequests Off
 ProxyPreserveHost On
 ProxyPass / https://localhost:8443/
 ProxyPassReverse / https://localhost:8443/
</VirtualHost>

https://host.example.org:8443 loads correctly. https://host.example.org does not. Firefox connects, then reports that the connection was interrupted.

Apache's error.log shows: "proxy: no HTTP 0.9 request (with no host line) on incoming request and preserve host set forcing hostname to be host.example.org for uri".

Tomcat's access log records an odd request line for these attempts: "?O^A^C / HTTP/1.1" 302. When I hit 8443 directly, the same log shows a normal "GET / HTTP/1.1" 302.

The same vhost pattern works when SSL is not involved at all.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The port-443 VirtualHost never enables SSL on the client-facing side: there is no SSLEngine on and no certificate or key. Apache therefore reads the browser's TLS handshake bytes as a plain (HTTP/0.9-style) request and forwards that garbage to Tomcat. Fix: Add SSLEngine on, plus SSLCertificateFile and SSLCertificateKeyFile, to the VirtualHost so Apache terminates TLS from the browser. Keep SSLProxyEngine On so Apache can still proxy to https://localhost:8443/.
solution: (1) The 443 vhost lacks SSLEngine on and a certificate/key, so it speaks plain HTTP to clients. (2) SSLProxyEngine only handles the backend connection; it does not enable TLS toward the browser. (3) The binary request line in Tomcat's log and the HTTP 0.9 warning are TLS handshake bytes being treated as HTTP. (4) Both SSLEngine (frontend) and SSLProxyEngine (backend) are needed.
technology: Apache httpd 2.2 mod_proxy / mod_ssl with Tomcat

grounding.title: Apache VirtualHost with mod-proxy and SSL

question:
We're building a Windows Server 2008 R2 / IIS7 box as a failover for our existing IIS6 web server, which we will later upgrade. Both need to serve our GoDaddy wildcard SSL cert (*.domain.com). That cert is already in production on the IIS6 machine. On the new server I downloaded the cert bundle from GoDaddy again. The zip contains two files: gd_iis_intermediates and a domain-named .crt. In IIS Manager I go to Server Certificates, choose 'Complete Certificate Request', point it at the domain .crt, give it a friendly name and finish. The cert appears in the list right away. After a refresh, or after navigating away and back, it is gone. It never shows up as a choice when I add an https binding to a site. If I try to complete the request with the intermediates file instead, I get: 'Cannot find the certificate request that is associated with this certificate file. A certificate request must be completed on the computer where the request was created.' People suggested exporting the cert as a .pfx from the IIS6 server and importing that. I couldn't find any way to export it there, and certmgr.msc didn't help either.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The certificate request, and therefore the private key, was originally generated on the IIS6 server. The new IIS7 server has no matching private key, so completing the request there fails silently and the cert drops out of the list. The existing cert on IIS6 was marked non-exportable, so its key could not be moved to the new server. Fix: Rekey the certificate in the GoDaddy account management page using a request generated on the IIS7 server, then complete it there. Export that certificate with its private key as a .pfx and import the .pfx on the IIS6 server so both servers use the same key pair.
solution: (1) Completing the request on a machine that didn't create the CSR leaves the cert without a private key, so it vanishes and can't be bound (2) The original cert's private key on IIS6 was not exportable, so it couldn't be moved as a .pfx (3) The cert must be rekeyed at GoDaddy and reinstalled (4) Export a .pfx with the private key from the server that completed the request, and import it on the other server
technology: IIS7 / Windows Server 2008 R2 SSL certificates

grounding.title: Installing SSL Certificate for use in IIS7, installation "works", but cert listing disappears

question:
Our PostgreSQL database host is an Ubuntu 12.04 Xen VM (kernel 3.2.0-43-virtual) with about 15 GB RAM and no swap. The OOM killer keeps killing postgres, even though our once-a-minute top snapshots show roughly 6.5 GB as 'cached'.

The last snapshots before the kill:
- Mem: 15339640k total, 15268304k used, 71336k free, 3152k buffers; 6608384k cached
- Mem: 15339640k total, 14855280k used, 484360k free, 13748k buffers; 6481852k cached

After postgres was killed, top showed 7127440k free and only 2394444k cached.

Syslog shows the trigger was a page fault in wal-e (the WAL archiver):
"wal-e invoked oom-killer: gfp_mask=0x201da, order=0"
The call trace runs through filemap_fault -> __page_cache_alloc -> out_of_memory.

The Mem-Info dump in the same log contains:
- "1615243 total pagecache pages"
- active_file:98 inactive_file:168

We expected the kernel to drop cache before killing anything. Why did the OOM killer fire with that much memory reported as cached?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The host genuinely ran out of memory. Most of the 'Cached' figure was PostgreSQL's shared memory (shared_buffers), which the kernel counts as page cache but cannot drop, and only a few hundred file-backed pages were actually reclaimable. Fix: Stop treating top's 'cached' value as available memory, and size the workload to the real memory. Do this by reducing PostgreSQL's memory footprint (e.g. shared_buffers and other memory settings) and/or adding RAM or swap so total demand fits.
solution: (1) The 'cached' value in top includes shared memory such as PostgreSQL shared_buffers, not just discardable disk cache (2) The OOM log's 1615243 pagecache pages x 4 KB (~6.48 GB) matches top's cached figure, so the cache was not dropped before the OOM kill (3) active_file and inactive_file are tiny (98 and 168 pages), so almost none of that 'cache' was reclaimable file-backed memory (4) The system was truly out of memory, so the remedy is lowering memory demand or adding capacity, not tuning the cache
technology: PostgreSQL on Linux (OOM killer / page cache)

grounding.title: OOM despite available memory (cache)

question:
Our hosting provider let the site's TLS certificate expire, then re-issued and installed a new one. Since then HTTPS works for me, for the host's staff, and for most users. About a dozen out of several hundred users still get "Your connection is not secure" across different browsers and operating systems. One of them runs exactly the same Firefox build I do (45.0.1 on OS X) and gets SEC_ERROR_UNKNOWN_ISSUER, but only on our site. He has cleared his cache and rebooted, and the error persists. I can't reproduce it on my own machine. An online checker (DigiCert's SSL tool, testing against Mozilla's root store) reports "SSL Certificate is not trusted: The certificate is not signed by a trusted authority." I don't understand how my browser connects without any warning if that result is correct.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: When the provider installed the new certificate, the server was left without the intermediate CA certificate(s), so it sends an incomplete chain. Clients that already have the intermediate cached or can obtain it some other way still build a path to the root. Clients that lack it cannot, and they fail with an unknown issuer error. Fix: Have the hosting provider install the intermediate certificate(s) supplied by the CA on the web server so the full chain is served. Then verify the result with a tool such as the SSL Labs server test.
solution: (1) The certificate chain served by the server is incomplete because the intermediate certificate is missing. (2) Whether a client fails depends on whether it can complete the chain itself (for example, a previously cached intermediate), which is why the same browser version behaves differently on different machines. (3) The fix is to install the CA-provided intermediate certificate(s) on the server.

grounding.title: How can an SSL certificate work for some clients only?

question:
We're loading a 30GB mysqldump into an empty database on a freshly built MySQL server. The server's my.cnf is essentially the stock config and hasn't been tuned yet. The import is being piped into the mysql client.

The load started out fast, but throughput has been dropping steadily as it goes. Individual INSERT statements from the dump now take 15 seconds or more each.

Most of the tables are MyISAM, plus one small InnoDB table. Nothing else is connected to the server. SHOW PROCESSLIST lists only the restore's INSERT and the PROCESSLIST query itself, so there is no lock contention or competing workload.

We want to know why the import keeps degrading the further it gets, and whether a server variable could be changed to speed up the rest of the restore while it is still running.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The MyISAM key buffer (key_buffer_size), which caches index blocks, is too small. As the tables and their indexes grow during the import, index updates for each insert spill to disk, so inserts get progressively slower. Fix: Increase key_buffer_size substantially, to roughly 30% or more of RAM, so MyISAM index maintenance during the load happens in memory. For InnoDB tables with foreign keys, you can also SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS=0 during the import and set it back to 1 afterwards.
solution: (1) Most tables are MyISAM, so index caching depends on key_buffer_size, not the InnoDB buffer pool. (2) The default or small key_buffer_size cannot hold the growing indexes, so index updates spill to disk and inserts slow down over time. (3) Raise key_buffer_size to around 30% or more of RAM to speed up the restore. (4) Optionally, disable FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS for InnoDB tables during the import and re-enable it afterwards.

grounding.title: How can I speed up a MySQL restore from a dump file?

question:
Workstation running Ubuntu 20.04 (Focal). Earlier today the user installed a Check Point SSL VPN client. Since then, every `sudo apt-get update` fails for all HTTPS repositories.

Local file: repos (a cuDNN local repo) still read fine. Every https source errors out on its Release file. Affected sources include dl.google.com (Chrome), dl.winehq.org, gitlab.com (feren-os repos), packages.microsoft.com (azure-cli, ms-teams), download.docker.com, desktop-download.mendeley.com and developer.download.nvidia.com.

Each one fails with the same message:

`Certificate verification failed: The certificate is NOT trusted. The certificate issuer is unknown. Could not handshake: Error in the certificate verification. [IP: 74.125.68.91 443]`

The IPs vary, and they belong to unrelated vendors and CDNs. The error is identical for every vendor. Nothing changed in the sources.list entries. The user can't install or update anything over HTTPS through apt.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer:
Root cause: The system's CA certificate trust store was corrupted or emptied, apparently while the VPN software was being installed. Certificate files were left without content, so no server certificate can be chained to a trusted root. Fix: 1. Manually download the ca-certificates .deb that matches your Ubuntu release from packages.ubuntu.com. You may need `wget --no-check-certificate`, since HTTPS validation is broken.
2. Remove the damaged package with `dpkg -r --force-depends ca-certificates`.
3. Reinstall it with `dpkg -i <package>.deb`. This restores a clean trust store.
solution: (1) The failure hits every HTTPS repo from unrelated vendors with 'issuer is unknown', so the fault is local rather than on the servers. (2) The local CA bundle/trust store (ca-certificates) is broken or empty, likely damaged by the VPN client install. (3) Fix by force-removing and reinstalling the ca-certificates package, using a .deb fetched without certificate checking.

grounding.title: Apt-Get Update Failing because of Certificate Validation

question:
We wanted to relax protected mode on our production Redis host svim-redis03. A Sentinel instance on another machine is being refused with "DENIED Redis is running in protected mode because protected mode is enabled, no bind address was specified, no authentication password is requested to clients...". That message suggests running 'CONFIG SET protected-mode no' from loopback, so we did:

127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG GET protected*
(empty list or set)
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG GET bind*
1) "bind" 2) "127.0.0.1"
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG SET protected-mode no
(error) ERR Unsupported CONFIG parameter: protected-mode

Changing bind fails the same way: config set bind "127.0.0.1 11.12.13.14" -> ERR Unsupported CONFIG parameter: bind. There is no auth configured. Access is controlled by firewall rules and redis.conf is close to default. `redis-server --version` reports v=3.2.9 (build 86450d2ba8219c1e). The docs and GitHub issues gave us nothing. Do runtime config changes need to be enabled somehow?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The Redis process actually listening on 6379 is an old instance (redis_version 3.0.7, up ~126 days) started before the package upgrade. It never restarted onto the installed 3.2.9 binary, and the old version does not support the protected-mode parameter or CONFIG SET bind. Fix: Confirm the running version with `INFO server`. Stop the service, use `ps` to verify the old redis-server PID is really gone (kill it if it is still alive), then start the service again. Check that INFO server now reports 3.2.9, after which the config parameters can be changed.
solution: (1) The running server version differs from the installed binary version reported by `redis-server --version` (2) INFO server shows redis_version 3.0.7 with a long uptime, meaning it was never restarted after the upgrade (3) The old version doesn't recognize protected-mode, which explains the 'Unsupported CONFIG parameter' error (4) The fix is to fully kill the stale process and restart it, then verify the version

grounding.title: How to turn off 'protected-mode' in Redis?

question:
A CentOS 5.5 guest runs PostgreSQL 8.4.4. A simple lookup is crawling:

SELECT * FROM consumer_m WHERE lower(last_name) = 'hoque';

The table has only varchar columns, and there is an expression index on lower(last_name). EXPLAIN shows a Bitmap Index Scan on consumer_m_last_name_index feeding a Bitmap Heap Scan, with about 113k estimated rows. Autovacuum is enabled, and no manual VACUUM or ANALYZE has been run.

While the query runs, `iostat -dxk 1 /dev/xvdb1` shows:
- r/s and w/s of either 0.00 or about 0.99–1.00
- rkB/s and wkB/s in single digits (about 4–8 kB/s)
- avgqu-sz between 1 and 2
- await around 1874–2220 ms
- svctm between 502 and 1004 ms
- %util pinned at 99–100% in every sample, even in seconds when zero I/Os completed

The disk reports itself as fully busy while moving almost no data. It is unclear why utilization and latency are so high when throughput is this low.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The bottleneck is below PostgreSQL. The xvdb1 device is a Xen virtual block device, and the underlying storage backing it is contended or otherwise performing very poorly. As a result, each I/O takes on the order of a second to be serviced. Fix: Investigate the Xen storage configuration and check for contention on the underlying physical device. Run iostat on the host/dom0 device as well as the guest. Then resolve the contention or reconfigure the storage, eliminating each layer in turn until the bottleneck is isolated.
solution: (1) The xvd* device name indicates a Xen guest using a virtual block device (2) About 1 IOPS with 100% util and ~2 s await means the storage layer, not the query plan, is the bottleneck (3) Contention or poor performance on the underlying host storage should be checked, e.g. iostat on dom0/backing device (4) Systematically eliminate each layer (DB, guest, hypervisor, physical disk) to isolate the problem

grounding.title: Extremely Slow IO with Simple PostgreSQL 8.4.4 Queries on Centos 5.5

question:
We're building a site-to-site IPsec tunnel with strongSwan 5.1.2 between two EC2 instances running Ubuntu 14.04.2. The N.Virginia instance is 10.198.0.164 with Elastic IP 54.X.X.X. The Oregon instance is 10.194.0.176 with Elastic IP 52.Y.Y.Y. Libreswan on a RedHat AMI worked earlier in a similar setup.

AWS-side checks done so far:
- Security groups and NACLs allow all traffic.
- Source/dest check is disabled on both instances.
- Routes point the remote 10.x range at the local instance.
- ip_forward=1 is set.

The Oregon ipsec.conf has left=52.Y.Y.Y, leftsubnet=10.194.0.0/16, right=54.X.X.X, rightsubnet=10.198.0.0/16, authby=secret, auto=start, type=tunnel, mobike=no, dpdaction=restart. N.Virginia mirrors it. ipsec.secrets holds a PSK keyed on the two EIPs.

IKE never comes up. Syslog on N.Virginia shows repeated retransmits:
```
[NET] sending packet: from 54.X.X.X[500] to 52.Y.Y.Y[500] (1212 bytes)
[NET] error writing to socket: Invalid argument
[IKE] giving up after 5 retransmits
[IKE] establishing IKE_SA failed, peer not responding
```

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: In a VPC, an instance's Elastic/public IP is NAT'd by AWS and never assigned to the instance's own network stack. Setting left= to the EIP makes charon try to send packets from an address the host doesn't own, which produces "error writing to socket: Invalid argument". Fix: Set left= and leftsourceip= to the instance's private IP, and set leftid= to the local Elastic IP. Keep right= as the remote Elastic IP on each side, along with the existing subnets.
solution: (1) The EIP/public IP is not configured on the instance's interface in a VPC (it is NAT'd by AWS) (2) charon tries to bind/send from the EIP, causing 'error writing to socket: Invalid argument' (3) left/leftsourceip must be the local private IP (4) leftid should be the local Elastic IP so identity/PSK matching still works

grounding.title: Strongswan VPN tunnel between two AWS instances won't connect

question:
We run several HTTP backends behind an AWS Elastic Load Balancer. Our Route53-hosted domain has a CNAME pointing to the ELB's DNS name. Clients in some locations, but not all, intermittently cannot connect. Other clients connect fine at the same time.

AWS support said the ELB's underlying IP had changed and that some ISP resolvers ignore TTLs. That doesn't fit what we see. We reproduced the failure:
- from an EC2 instance using Amazon's own resolver
- from several Australian ISPs
- through Google DNS (8.8.8.8)

On the failing machines, the name resolves to an IP that looks correct, but the TCP connection to that IP never establishes. AWS confirmed that traffic through the ELB dropped sharply during the outage windows. Every backend instance registered with the ELB reported healthy the whole time.

We can't tell where the failure is or how to dig deeper.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: An ELB is made up of multiple load-balancer nodes, each published as a separate A record under the ELB's DNS name. One or more of these nodes had failed or stopped responding while still being handed out in DNS. Clients whose resolver returned the bad node's IP could not open a TCP connection, even though the backends were healthy. Fix: Resolve the full list of ELB nodes, for example with `dig +tcp <elb-name> ANY` against Amazon's nameserver or `dig all.<elb-name>`. Test each node IP individually without reaching the backends: send an HTTP method longer than 127 characters with curl and expect a 405 from the ELB itself, or use the elbping tool. Report the unresponsive node IPs to AWS support so they can be replaced.
solution: (1) An ELB consists of multiple nodes, each exposed as a separate A record under the ELB name (2) A single failed node still published in DNS causes only some clients to fail, even though DNS resolution looks correct (3) Each node IP must be tested individually, isolated from the backends (e.g., an oversized HTTP method returns 405 from the ELB, or elbping) (4) Healthy backends do not rule out a problem at the ELB node layer
technology: AWS Elastic Load Balancer / Route53 DNS

grounding.title: Issues with EC2 Elastic Load Balancer DNS and routing

question:
After an in-place upgrade of a minimal CentOS 7 box to CentOS 8, I enabled and started firewalld. systemctl status shows it active (running) with no errors. I added http and ssh services both at runtime and with --permanent. firewall-cmd --list-all on zone public (active, interface eth0) lists services: http ssh. However, iptables -nvL shows completely empty INPUT, FORWARD and OUTPUT chains, all with policy ACCEPT, and packet counters going up on INPUT. Rebooting changes nothing; still no rules appear in iptables. Other CentOS 7 servers I manage show firewalld rules in iptables as expected. I never tested firewalld on this host before the upgrade. Is the upgrade broken, and where can I look to debug why no rules are being created?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: Nothing is broken: on CentOS 8 firewalld uses nftables as its backend instead of iptables, so its rules are not visible in the legacy iptables listing. The iptables command itself is the nf_tables compatibility variant and only shows its own (empty) tables. Fix: Inspect the active rules with `nft list ruleset`; the ssh/http rules appear in the chain filter_IN_public_allow (e.g. 'tcp dport ssh ct state new,untracked accept'). No repair is needed.
solution: (1) firewalld in CentOS 8 uses nftables backend, not iptables (2) iptables -nvL won't show firewalld rules; use nft list ruleset (3) rules appear in chains like filter_IN_public_allow (4) iptables v1.8 is the nf_tables variant (iptables -V shows nf_tables)

grounding.title: firewalld is not working in CentOS 8: no rule at all is created in iptables

question:
Our Ubuntu 8.04 iptables gateway NATs internal clients (e.g. 192.168.126.161) out through its external address 10.1.1.1. For a long time some HTTP requests through it have hung half-loaded until TCP times out. Captures on both sides of the box show a timing pattern.

- The handshake completes and the GET is sent and ACKed.
- The first response segment (200 OK, text/css) is forwarded to the client, which ACKs it.
- The web server (172.16.1.2) then sends the rest of the body in one burst of about 8 segments, ending with FIN/PSH, before the client has ACKed any of them.
- Most of these segments are forwarded normally to 192.168.126.161.
- The final segment is never forwarded. Instead, the gateway itself sends a RST from 10.1.1.1:37854 to 172.16.1.2:80.
- The client is left waiting forever.

This only happens when the server finishes sending before the client's second ACK arrives. Normal-paced transfers are fine. Why is the gateway resetting the connection instead of forwarding the last packet?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: Some packets of the flow are classified by netfilter conntrack as INVALID instead of ESTABLISHED. INVALID packets are not NAT-translated, so they are delivered to the firewall's INPUT chain and local stack. The local stack has no matching socket and responds with a RST to the web server. Fix: Drop INVALID packets before they reach the local stack, e.g. `iptables -I INPUT -m state --state INVALID -j DROP`. TCP will then retransmit and recover instead of being reset. Debug why the packets are INVALID with `echo 255 > /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_log_invalid`. In the similar case referenced, the cause was faulty network hardware or TCP checksum offload.
solution: (1) conntrack marks the packet INVALID rather than ESTABLISHED (2) INVALID packets are not NAT'd and end up in the firewall's INPUT chain/local stack, which generates the RST from 10.1.1.1 (3) Drop INVALID-state packets with iptables (-m state --state INVALID -j DROP) (4) Enable nf_conntrack_log_invalid to see why packets are considered invalid

grounding.title: Why is our firewall (Ubuntu 8.04) rejecting the final packet (FIN, ACK, PSH) with a RST

question:
We run MySQL in a Docker container on an Ubuntu host with Docker 0.7.3 (client and server, go1.2). The image is based on ubuntu:12.10. It sets bind-address = 0.0.0.0 in my.cnf, grants root@'%', and has EXPOSE 3306. We start it with `docker run -p 3306:3306 asyncfi/magento-mysql`.

Local logins work, but remote machines can also log in to MySQL, which we did not intend. The host firewall is meant to allow only a hidden SSH port plus HTTP and HTTPS. As a test, a Django dev server listening on port 1234 is reachable locally but not from outside, so the filtering appears to work for normal processes.

`iptables -L -v` shows:
- INPUT: ACCEPT on lo, ACCEPT for RELATED,ESTABLISHED, ACCEPT on the SSH, http and https ports, then LOG and DROP everything else (the DROP rule has around 551 packets).
- FORWARD: policy ACCEPT, with docker0-related ACCEPT rules.
- OUTPUT: policy ACCEPT.

Why is the containerized MySQL reachable from the outside network when the firewall should block port 3306?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The container was started with `-p 3306:3306`, which publishes the container port on all of the host's interfaces. Docker's own port publishing therefore makes MySQL reachable externally regardless of the INPUT filtering rules. Fix: Publish the port only on the loopback address, e.g. `docker run -p 127.0.0.1:3306:3306 asyncfi/magento-mysql`. The EXPOSE line in the Dockerfile is not needed for this, since it only matters for container linking.
solution: (1) `-p 3306:3306` without an IP binds the published port on all host interfaces (2) this is why the port is externally reachable despite the host INPUT DROP rules (3) fix by specifying the host IP: `-p 127.0.0.1:3306:3306` (4) EXPOSE is not what publishes the port to the host

grounding.title: Why does a Docker container running a server expose port to the outside world even though said port is blocked by iptables?

question:
A new OpenVPN server (UDP 1194, tun, server 10.8.0.0/24, client-to-client, redirect-gateway def1) is running on a host at 192.168.0.250. The server config includes these lines:

push "route 10.8.0.1 255.255.255.255"
push "route 10.8.0.0 255.255.255.0"
push "route 192.168.0.250 255.255.255.0"
push "dhcp-option DNS 8.8.8.8"
push "redirect-gateway def1"

A Linux client running OpenVPN 2.3.2 connects with `openvpn --config myfile.ovpn`. The peer connection initiates and tun0 opens. The client runs `/sbin/ip addr add dev tun0 local 10.8.0.14 peer 10.8.0.13`. Right after that the log shows:

RTNETLINK answers: Invalid argument
ERROR: Linux route add command failed: external program exited with error status: 2
RTNETLINK answers: File exists
ERROR: Linux route add command failed: external program exited with error status: 2
Initialization Sequence Completed

The connection comes up, but the route errors appear on every connect. Find out why the client's route additions fail.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The server pushes bad routes to the client. Two routes cover the tunnel's own 10.8.0.0/24 address pool, which OpenVPN already handles, and they overlap each other, so the add hits 'File exists'. The third, 192.168.0.250 with mask 255.255.255.0, is an invalid host/netmask combination for the server's local net, which gives 'Invalid argument'. Fix: Remove the three push "route ..." lines from the server config and restart the server. Use push route only for other private subnets behind the server, written as network address plus mask (e.g. 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0).
solution: (1) The pushed routes for 10.8.0.1/32 and 10.8.0.0/24 are the tunnel's own VPN range, which OpenVPN sets up automatically, so pushing them is unnecessary and conflicting. (2) 10.8.0.1 is inside 10.8.0.0/24, so the two pushed routes are redundant and collide ('File exists'). (3) 'route 192.168.0.250 255.255.255.0' uses a host address with a /24 mask, which is invalid ('Invalid argument'); the local net doesn't need to be pushed anyway. (4) push route is meant for additional private subnets behind the server.

grounding.title: VPN: ERROR: Linux route add command failed

question:
After the January 2018 Meltdown/Spectre patch round, two CentOS 7 hosts were updated to kernel-3.10.0-693.11.6.el7.x86_64 and microcode_ctl-2.1-22.2.el7.x86_64, then rebooted. The CPU is an Intel Xeon D-1540 (Broadwell, family 6, model 86, stepping 2).

Verification via the debugfs tunables shows:
- /sys/kernel/debug/x86/pti_enabled = 1
- ibpb_enabled = 0
- ibrs_enabled = 0

Trying to turn them on fails. For example, `echo 1 > /sys/kernel/debug/x86/ibrs_enabled` returns "-bash: echo: write error: No such device", and ibpb_enabled gives the same error.

The microcode.service unit ran successfully at boot (status=0/SUCCESS). dmesg shows the microcode driver loading on all 16 CPUs with "sig=0x50662, pf=0x10, revision=0xf". /proc/cpuinfo still reports "microcode : 0xf".

The flags list in cpuinfo does not show anything obviously branch-speculation related. Page table isolation appears active, but the other two mitigation knobs refuse to be enabled. Why are only some of the mitigations working?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: Spectre variant 2 (CVE-2017-5715) mitigations controlled by ibrs_enabled/ibpb_enabled require CPU microcode that exposes IBRS/IBPB support. This CPU is still running microcode revision 0xf, which lacks it. The kernel therefore has no IBRS/IBPB capability to enable, hence "No such device", while PTI (Meltdown) needs only the kernel. Fix: Obtain and apply updated microcode for this CPU from the hardware vendor, typically via a BIOS/firmware update. Then reboot and recheck that ibrs_enabled and ibpb_enabled read 1.
