solution: (1) Spectre v2 (CVE-2017-5715) needs both a kernel patch and updated CPU microcode (2) The ibrs/ibpb tunables only work in conjunction with microcode support; PTI needs only the kernel (3) The loaded microcode (rev 0xf) does not provide IBRS/IBPB for this CPU, so the writes fail with 'No such device' (4) A microcode/BIOS update from the hardware vendor is required
technology: CentOS 7 / RHEL 7 kernel, Intel CPU microcode (Meltdown/Spectre mitigations)

grounding.title: I updated my CentOS 7 system. Why is Meltdown/Spectre only partially mitigated?

question:
Hobby setup: a Minecraft server runs in a Windows container based on Windows Server Core 2022 on a Windows host.

Started manually with `docker run -it -p 25565:25565 --mount type=bind,source="C:\MinecraftDocker\MinecraftServer",target=C:/MinecraftServer minecraft:winserver2022`, everything works.

Started with docker-compose using the same image, the container and server process come up normally. The compose service defines build context, `platform: windows`, `restart: unless-stopped`, port 25565 and the same bind mount. Clients can reach the server, and their account names show in the console. But every login fails with a message claiming the Mojang authentication servers are down, which they are not.

Further testing inside the compose-started container:
- Every hostname lookup fails.
- Pinging the auth servers' IP addresses directly succeeds.
- In the docker run container, name resolution works fine.

Stripping the compose file down to just context, ports and volumes changed nothing. A nearly identical compose file for Linux containers on the same host has no problem.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: docker-compose attaches the container to a network it creates for the project, and the container uses that network's gateway as its DNS server. That gateway only answers with 'server failed'. docker run uses the default network and inherits the host's DNS configuration, so resolution works there. Fix: Override the container's DNS server in the compose service definition, e.g. `dns: <reachable DNS server IP>`. Name resolution then works normally.
solution: (1) The failure is DNS-only; IP connectivity works (2) The compose-started container uses the gateway of the compose-generated network as its DNS server, and it returns SERVFAIL (3) docker run uses the default network and inherits the host DNS settings, which is why it works (4) Setting `dns:` explicitly in the compose service resolves it

grounding.title: DNS resolution fails when container is started via docker-compose

question:
I'm setting up a docker-compose project on Ubuntu 19. The first service is MySQL, using image mysql:5.7, and my app will depend on it. Compose file (version 3.3):

```
services:
  db:
    image: mysql:5.7
    volumes:
      - ./tmp/db:/var/lib/mysql
    restart: always
    environment:
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: root
      MYSQL_DATABASE: wordpress
      MYSQL_USER: wordpress
      MYSQL_PASSWORD: wordpress
```

The container starts. I exec into it with `docker exec -it <container> bash` and run the mysql client with the configured credentials. It always fails:

```
ERROR 1045 (28000): Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost' (using password: YES)
```

The wordpress user fails the same way:

```
ERROR 1045 (28000): Access denied for user 'wordpress'@'localhost' (using password: YES)
```

I've spent hours changing the passwords and environment settings and recreating the container. Nothing changes the result. I'm starting to suspect the image itself is broken.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The bind-mounted ./tmp/db directory already contains an initialized MySQL data directory from an earlier run. The image's entrypoint skips initialization when it finds an existing database, so the MYSQL_* environment variables are ignored and the old users and passwords are still in effect. Fix: Stop the container and delete all files and directories in ./tmp/db. Then start the project again so MySQL initializes a fresh data directory with the credentials from docker-compose.yml.
solution: (1) The compose file and image are fine; it works with an empty data directory (2) ./tmp/db holds a pre-existing initialized MySQL database from a previous run (3) The MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD/MYSQL_USER/MYSQL_PASSWORD env vars only apply when the data directory is empty (4) Clearing the host data directory and restarting fixes it

grounding.title: Can't make MySQL 5.7 work with Docker Compose, no matter what

question:
We run an Aurora MySQL cluster in our default VPC. Two EKS 1.18 clusters need to reach it on 3306: eks-cluster-working and eks-cluster-broken. The environment VPC(s) are connected to the default VPC through a VPC peering connection that Terraform creates (aws_vpc_peering_connection with auto_accept = true). Terraform also builds a route table in the default VPC with a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the IGW plus routes to each environment CIDR via the peering connection.

The RDS security group has two inbound rules for MYSQL/Aurora TCP 3306. One uses the working cluster's EKS security group as its source, and connections through it succeed. The other uses the broken cluster's EKS security group as its source, and connections from that cluster's pods never get through.

Both clusters use the default EKS-created security groups. The only extra one is a load balancer SG on the working cluster, which serves a web app. Both have outbound rules to 0.0.0.0/0. There are no AWS Network Firewall policies or rule groups in the region.

The two clusters look equivalent from a security-group standpoint, so we can't explain why only one of them can reach the database. What should we check?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The peering connection's DNS setting that lets the accepter VPC resolve the requester (default) VPC's hostnames to private IPs was disabled. From the broken cluster, the RDS endpoint therefore resolved to its public address, so the traffic did not go over the peering connection and the security-group-based rule did not apply. Fix: In the VPC peering connection, choose Actions -> Edit DNS Settings and enable 'Allow accepter VPC to resolve DNS of requester VPC hosts to private IP'. Then wait a short while for the change to propagate. In Terraform, the equivalent is setting allow_remote_vpc_dns_resolution in the peering connection's accepter options.
solution: (1) The RDS endpoint is a DNS name that must resolve to a private IP for traffic to use the peering connection (2) The VPC peering DNS resolution option for the accepter VPC was disabled (3) Without it, the hostname resolves to a public IP, so the SG rule referencing the peered cluster's security group never matches (4) Fix: enable 'allow accepter VPC to resolve DNS of requester VPC hosts to private IP' on the peering connection
technology: AWS VPC peering / EKS / Aurora RDS

grounding.title: K8s cluster in peered VPC can't reach RDS cluster

question:
I'm setting up Helm (v2, with Tiller) on a kubeadm-built cluster for the first time. I created a tiller service account bound to cluster-admin and ran `helm init --service-account=tiller`. Both steps succeeded.

Since then, almost every Helm command fails, including `helm install stable/kibana`, installing gitlab/gitlab-runner from an added repo, and even `helm list`. Each one hangs and then returns:

```
Error: forwarding ports: error upgrading connection: error dialing backend: dial tcp 192.168.0.18:10250: getsockopt: connection timed out
```

The address 192.168.0.18 belongs to worker node kube-worker-7. The kube-proxy and weave-net pods on that node show that IP. The tiller-deploy pod is Running on the same node with pod IP 10.38.0.1.

Someone suggested I was missing RBAC rights for port-forwarding or listing pods. However, `kubectl auth can-i create pods/portforward` and `kubectl auth can-i list pods` both return yes. The nodes are hosts whose 192.168.x addresses are on their local network.

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: When the nodes joined via kubeadm, the kubelet registered them with their private IPs (192.168.x.x). The master cannot route to those addresses. So when the API server dials the kubelet on port 10250 to set up Helm's port-forward to Tiller, the connection times out. Fix: Edit /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf on each node and add `--node-ip=<public-node-ip>` to the kubelet arguments. Then run `systemctl daemon-reload`, restart the kubelet, and re-register the nodes so they advertise a reachable IP.
solution: (1) The failure is network reachability from the API server/master to the kubelet on port 10250, not RBAC. (2) The nodes advertised private 192.168.x IPs that the master cannot reach. (3) Helm v2 uses port-forwarding through the API server to the kubelet to reach Tiller, so all commands fail. (4) Set the kubelet `--node-ip` to the reachable/public IP in 10-kubeadm.conf, then reload, restart and re-register the nodes.

grounding.title: Why does Helm time out on almost every action?

question:
After upgrading the Jenkins controller from 2.39 to 2.57, none of our SSH-launched build agents will connect. Each launch attempt gets as far as the remoting banner and then fails:

```
<===[JENKINS REMOTING CAPACITY]===>channel started
Slave JVM has not reported exit code. Is it still running?
Launch failed - cleaning up connection
[SSH] Connection closed.
ERROR: Connection terminated
java.io.EOFException
 at java.io.ObjectInputStream$PeekInputStream.readFully(...)
 at hudson.remoting.ObjectInputStreamEx.<init>(...)
 at hudson.remoting.SynchronousCommandTransport$ReaderThread.run(...)
Caused: java.io.IOException: Unexpected termination of the channel
```

Before the upgrade the same agents worked fine. Searching the error turned up older reports blaming a mismatched Java install on the agent. I checked the agents and they consistently report:

```
$ java -version
java version "1.7.0_80"
Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 1.7.0_80-b15)
Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 24.80-b11, mixed mode)
```

So the agents all use the same Java version, and no agent config was changed. What is preventing the agents from coming up?

What is the most likely root cause, and how would you fix it?
answer: Root cause: The newer Jenkins version (2.54 and later, so including 2.57) requires Java 8. The agent JVMs are still Java 7, so the remoting agent process dies as soon as it starts and the channel terminates with an EOFException. Fix: Upgrade Java on all build agents to Java 8, or point the node's JVM/Java path setting at a Java 8 install. Then relaunch the agents.
solution: (1) Jenkins 2.54+ (including 2.57) requires Java 8 (2) Agents are running Java 1.7, which is no longer supported (3) Agent JVM fails at startup, causing 'Slave JVM has not reported exit code' and EOFException (4) Fix is upgrading agent Java to 8

grounding.title: Jenkins cannot reach nodes after upgrade
